project_claim_under_test: An RK3588 controller can use multiple cheap original RV1126 nodes as a decoder/expansion fabric for sparse generative-video state, with RV1126 nodes handling interpolation/residual-correction-class neural work and surrounding video operations.

project_specific_evidence.f1_f4: software theory, graph conversion, calibration and trained-reference quality are proven in the project evidence chain
project_specific_evidence.f5_static_preflight: PASS against the pinned original RKNPU1 1.7.5 header

source.measurement_scope: model inference at maximum NPU frequency; preprocessing and postprocessing excluded unless specified

conservative_published_silicon_compariso.surrogate: official original-RV1126 YOLOv5s 640x640 INT8 at 20 FPS
conservative_published_silicon_compariso.interpretation: The four-node fabric only needs 13.75 FPS/node in the hardest sparse-rate case. Rockchip publishes 20 FPS on original RV1126 for a mainstream 640x640 INT8 network, and substantially higher rates for several other networks. This is real-silicon evidence that the required per-node throughput regime is plausible. It does not prove that the exact F4 seven-channel residual graph achieves 13.75 FPS or better.

latency_boundary.reason: Frame-parallel nodes increase aggregate throughput but do not shorten one model invocation; sparse interpolation also implies buffering/future-anchor considerations.

feasibility_judgement.next_discriminator: Run F5A and F5B on one original RV1126. If the exact F4 model executes correctly and sustains at least 13.75 reconstructed FPS/node, the four-node compute-throughput premise is directly supported for the hardest 5->60 case. If below that threshold, test 8-node economics or reduce the model before claiming the architecture.
